activities.caption: call the house size of the Globe
activities.name: shkGlobeEstimate

config.prompt: Built in 1599, the Globe was a daylight, open-air amphitheatre. Roughly how many spectators could it hold?
config.why: Roughly three thousand — a yard of groundlings and galleries of gentry in one daylight space, which is why the plays braid lyrical verse for the connoisseurs with bawdy jokes and swordfights for the yard.
config.context: Storms, ghosts and battles were narrated in words rather than built with effects: the language had to do the scenery.

activities.caption: true or false — the registers of the set text
activities.name: shkRegisterJudge

statements.s: The Tempest's opening storm is done entirely in shouting prose and broken lines.
statements.why: Chaos below decks — the boatswain's "Blow till thou burst thy wind, if room enough!"

statements.s: Prospero, backstage, calmly explains the storm in verse because the storm is his.
statements.why: Control above decks — the verse carries the power.

statements.s: Caliban speaks prose because he is labelled a savage slave.
statements.why: The registers cut against the social labels on purpose: Caliban speaks some of the most beautiful verse in the play — "Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises" — while the drunken butler Stephano speaks prose.

statements.s: Noticing where a speech sits on the verse-prose dial is often the whole answer.
statements.why: Shakespeare's registers are deliberate, and the dial position is information.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the same line, loaded and unloaded
activities.name: shkIronyCompare

config.prompt: One line, two knowledge states — drag the divider:

before.label: The line unloaded
before.text: A line in a disguise plot, spoken to a character who does not know who they are talking to. On the stage, only the script and the spectators hold both identities at once.

after.label: The line loaded
after.text: The same line with the audience's knowledge behind it — the audience knows what half the cast does not, so ordinary lines become loaded, and an entire plot can run on double identities (Bunburying).

config.why: Prospero stages a playwright: his "art" is theatre itself, with a tempest as its opening act and forgiveness as its closing scene.

activities.anchor: The dictionary credits him with about 1,700
activities.caption: find the line the footnote corrects
activities.name: shkHoardSpot

config.prompt: One line of this word-hoard report is wrong — click it:
lines: The OED credits Shakespeare with about 1,700 first recorded uses.
Every one of those words was invented by him out of nothing.
Many were probably already in circulation — he is the earliest writer we can catch using them.
The deeper achievement is capture: familiar words in combinations no one had dared.
"Break the ice" and "wild-goose chase" are his coinages still in daily use.
config.correction: They are first recorded uses, not inventions from nothing — the real invention is combination, ordinary words under unprecedented pressure.
config.why: When you meet a startling phrase in a set speech, do not paraphrase it away: the strangeness is usually the sense.

config.prompt: Rebuild the five-act map, act by act:
items: Act 1 — the storm and the back-story
Act 2 — the shipwrecked court's treachery comedy
Act 3 — two plots of usurpation (Caliban's and Antonio's) converging
Act 4 — the masque and its interruption
config.why: Three plots run at different moral temperatures (comic, menacing, tender) and are intercut for contrast — a structural technique straight out of the novel lesson.

config.root: Every pronoun choice is a relationship reading — walk the dial through one court scene.

start.text: A courtier addresses the king at court. Which setting does the dial open on?

choices.label: thou
choices.feedback: The intimate, inferior-addressed or insulting form.

you-king.text: "You" — polite and distant, the default for a king. Now the betrayal scene: the same courtier, the same king, one line later. The dial moves to…

choices.label: thou
choices.feedback: The switch itself is the event.

thou-king.text: Thou to a king from the first line — that is already a reading: intimate, inferior-addressed or insulting before anything happens. The dial has spoken in grammar.

thou-betrayal.text: Thou at the moment of betrayal — the relationship event is audible in the grammar itself, the way Lear's "Thou art a boil" delivers the insult as syntax.

you-still.text: Holding "you" keeps the distance — no insult lands in the grammar, and the relationship reads as formal even in treachery.

config.why: Misreading the dial flips the very relationship the scene is staging — mark every thou/you switch; each is worth a sentence of analysis.

activities.caption: rebuild the reading method for a major speech
activities.name: shkSpeechOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the template for reading any major speech:
items: Find the question the speech opens with — ten syllables of monosyllables, the meter perfectly regular because the mind is trying to be logical.
Map how it argues — the case ("to die, to sleep"), the counter-case ("perchance to dream — ay, there's the rub"), the evidence (the whips and scorns of time).
Identify where the argument breaks — "conscience does make cowards of us all", a verdict that is no verdict.
Read the break as the character — no stage direction says "conflicted"; the failed structure performs it.
config.why: The syntax, the meter and the failed structure of the argument do what no bracketed direction could.

activities.anchor: Counting Shakespeare's lines shows a career-long
activities.caption: which curve matches the verse statistics?
activities.name: shkMeterTrace

config.prompt: One career of verse, scanned statistically — which profile matches what counting the lines shows?
config.why: Early plays are tightly end-stopped; the late plays run sentences over line breaks, weaken the caesura and add extra syllables — statistics regular enough to date undated plays and identify collaborators.
